name: The Epic of Gilgamesh
teaser: The oldest surviving work of literature — written 4,000 years ago on clay tablets, it already contains a flood story that predates Noah, and the hero's quest for immortality ends with him learning to accept death.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the tablet where Gilgamesh loses his best friend Enkidu — the grief is the point. The story's genius is that the hero's 'greatness' is his willingness to be mortal.

name: The Trojan War
teaser: A ten-year war fought over a woman — or over trade routes, depending on the historian — and the only surviving account is a poem about the anger of one man, not the war itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Iliad's opening scene — the rage of Achilles is the plot, and the war is the backdrop. The story's genius is that the 'hero' is the one who refuses to fight.

name: The Odyssey
teaser: Homer's epic about a man trying to get home for 10 years — every monster he meets is a version of the temptation to give up, and the poem's real subject is memory: who remembers you while you're gone.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the encounter with the Sirens — the hero has himself tied to the mast so he can hear the song without dying. The story's genius is that the 'home' he returns to is strangers.

name: Ragnarök
teaser: The Norse apocalypse — the gods know it's coming and prepare anyway, and the world is destroyed and reborn. Unlike most mythologies, Norse gods are mortal, which is the point.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the prophecy of Ragnarök and notice the gods prepare without hope. The story's genius is that the doom IS the theology: courage in the face of certain loss.

name: Odin's Sacrifice
teaser: The All-Father hung himself from Yggdrasil for nine days to learn the runes — the sacrifice of self for knowledge is the template for every 'forbidden wisdom' story since.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Havamal passage where Odin describes hanging from the tree — the 'wounded by spear, offered to Odin, myself to myself' line is the thesis. The story's genius is that wisdom costs the self.

name: Thor's Hammer
teaser: The hammer Mjolnir was forged by dwarves after Loki's bet — the story where Thor has to dress as a bride to get it back is the funniest myth in the Norse canon, and the hammer's 'worthiness' was added by Marvel.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the story of Thor's stolen hammer and the bridal disguise — the gods' embarrassment is the comedy. The story's genius is that the 'mightiest god' wins by being ridiculous.

name: Anansi the Spider
teaser: The Akan trickster god of stories — Anansi is a spider who outwits gods and kings with his wits, and the name of the Ashanti people's storytelling tradition comes from his name.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the story where Anansi captures the world's wisdom in a pot — the pot is too heavy to carry alone. The story's genius is that the 'wisdom' is in the sharing.

name: The Rainbow Serpent
teaser: The creator of the Dreamtime — the serpent shaped the land with its body, and the rivers are its tracks. The story is told on rock art thousands of years old.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the creation story and notice the land IS the story — the hills and rivers are the serpent's body. The myth's genius is that the landscape is the scripture.

name: Maui and the Sun
teaser: The demigod Maui snared the sun with ropes woven from his sister's hair to slow it down so people could cook — the story is a founding myth of everyday convenience.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the version where Maui beats the sun into submission — the 'sun's legs' are the ropes. The myth's genius is that the hero's prize is a longer day, not a treasure.

name: The Legend of King Arthur
teaser: The once and future king — whether he existed is debated, but the legend of the sword in the stone, Camelot and the Round Table shaped Western ideas of leadership for a thousand years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the sword-in-the-stone scene and notice what makes Arthur king — not strength but restraint. The legend's genius is that the 'rightful king' is the one who doesn't want the crown.

name: Excalibur
teaser: The Lady of the Lake's sword — in the oldest versions, Arthur's first sword breaks and Excalibur is a replacement, and the sword's scabbard (not the blade) is the magic part.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the scene where Excalibur is returned to the lake — the hand rises to catch it. The legend's genius is that the sword must be given back, not kept.

name: Robin Hood
teaser: The outlaw of Sherwood Forest — the 'robbing the rich to feed the poor' is a 16th-century addition, and the earliest ballads are about a yeoman defending his dignity against a sheriff's corruption.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the oldest ballad ('Robin Hood and the Monk') and notice Robin loses — the early stories are not invincible-hero fantasies. The legend's genius is that the outlaw is the law.

name: Beowulf
teaser: The oldest surviving English epic — the hero fights three monsters across his life, and the poem's real subject is what happens when the 'hero' grows old and the monster returns.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the dragon fight at the end — the aged hero wins but dies. The poem's genius is that the third monster is time itself.

name: The Minotaur
teaser: The half-bull half-man in the labyrinth — the maze was built by Daedalus to hide a royal shame, and Theseus navigates it with Ariadne's thread, the first 'unwinnable maze' solution in fiction.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Theseus story and notice the thread — the solution is not strength but a guide. The myth's genius is that the labyrinth is the mind.

name: Icarus
teaser: The boy who flew too close to the sun — his father Daedalus built the wings, and the wax melted. The warning 'don't fly too high' was added later; the original moral is about youth ignoring craft.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the story and notice Daedalus' instructions — he warns about BOTH extremes, too high and too low. The myth's genius is that the tragedy is the middle path ignored.

name: Pandora's Box
teaser: The first woman in Greek myth opened a jar (not a box — a mistranslation) releasing all evils — but Hope remained inside, and the myth's real question is whether hope is a comfort or a curse.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the version where Hope stays in the jar — the ambiguity is the point. The myth's genius is that the 'evils' are the human condition, and hope is the unresolved part.

name: Prometheus
teaser: The Titan who stole fire for humanity and was chained to a rock to have his liver eaten daily — the liver grew back, making his torment eternal, and his crime was 'thinking ahead' (his name means Forethought).

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Aeschylus play fragment where Prometheus refuses to apologize — the defiance is the character. The myth's genius is that the 'crime' is progress.

name: Medusa
teaser: The snake-haired Gorgon whose gaze turns men to stone — the oldest versions have no backstory; the 'cursed by Poseidon in Athena's temple' version came later, and her face was worn on shields as armor.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the oldest reference in the Iliad — Medusa is just a face on a shield. The myth's genius is that the monster is the armor.

name: Perseus
teaser: The only Greek hero who gets a happy ending — he beheads Medusa using a mirrored shield, and his story is the template for 'the hero's journey' before Campbell codified it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Gorgon fight and notice Perseus uses the reflection, never looking directly — the indirect approach is the method. The myth's genius is that the 'mirror' is the strategy.

name: The Twelve Labors of Hercules
teaser: The punishment for madness became the greatest quest list in myth — the labors (Nemean Lion, Hydra, Augean Stables...) are designed to be impossible, and Hercules wins some by trickery, not strength.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Augean Stables labor — Hercules diverts two rivers instead of shoveling. The myth's genius is that the 'strength' is intelligence.

name: Theseus and the Labyrinth
teaser: The hero who volunteered to be tribute — his thread through the maze is the origin of 'to find one's way', and the ending (abandoning Ariadne) is one of myth's crueler moments.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the story and notice Ariadne — she's the strategist, he's the muscle. The myth's genius is that the 'hero' is the one with the thread.

name: Orpheus and Eurydice
teaser: The musician whose song moved the underworld — he was allowed to lead his wife out on one condition: don't look back. He looked. The myth is the template for every 'don't look' horror rule.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the moment of the look back — the doubt is the tragedy. The myth's genius is that the 'condition' is the test of trust, and he fails it.

name: Narcissus
teaser: The youth who fell in love with his reflection and drowned reaching for it — the flower that bears his name grows where he died, and 'narcissism' is the modern inheritance.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the story and notice the reflection never loves back — the 'other' is a mirror. The myth's genius is that the self-love is self-loss.

name: Sisyphus
teaser: The king condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever — his crime was cheating death TWICE, and Camus' essay made him the patron saint of the absurd: the struggle itself is the meaning.

exploreAction.instruction: Read Camus' last line — 'one must imagine Sisyphus happy'. The myth's genius is that the punishment is the metaphor for every human project.

name: Daedalus and Icarus
teaser: The master craftsman who built the labyrinth and then escaped it with wings — the same genius who built the prison built the escape, and his son's fall is the cost of invention.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the escape scene and notice Daedalus watches his son die and keeps flying — the grief and the craft continue. The myth's genius is that the inventor is responsible for the invention.

name: The Phoenix
teaser: The bird that dies in flame and rises from its own ashes — the image appears in Egypt, Greece, Rome, and China independently, and the 'phoenix' is the most translated symbol in world myth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Greek version where the phoenix is a bird that lives 500 years — the 'rebirth' is the promise. The myth's genius is that the symbol outlives every telling.

name: Anubis
teaser: The jackal-headed god of the dead — jackals were seen at graves, so the god who guards the dead was given their head, and Anubis weighs the heart against a feather in the judgment hall.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Weighing of the Heart scene — the feather is the truth test. The myth's genius is that the 'judgment' is a balance, not a rulebook.

name: Osiris and Isis
teaser: The first resurrection myth in history — Osiris is dismembered and reassembled by Isis, and every Egyptian pharaoh's afterlife reenacts his story. The myth is 5,000 years old.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the reassembly scene and notice the missing piece — Osiris is incomplete. The myth's genius is that the 'resurrection' is a mending, not a miracle.

name: The Eye of Horus
teaser: The eye torn out in a fight and restored — the Wedjat eye became the symbol of healing, and the 'eye' hieroglyph is the origin of the Rx symbol used in pharmacies today.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the fight between Horus and Set — the eye's restoration is the plot. The myth's genius is that the 'healing' symbol is a wound made whole.

name: The Monkey King
teaser: Sun Wukong — the stone-born monkey who learned 72 transformations and caused havoc in heaven until Buddha trapped him under a mountain for 500 years — is the hero of the 16th-century epic 'Journey to the West'.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the scene where Sun Wukong challenges Buddha — the monkey tries to escape the Buddha's palm. The epic's genius is that the 'defeat' is the beginning of the journey.

name: The Jade Emperor
teaser: The supreme ruler of heaven in Chinese mythology — his court is a bureaucracy, and the myth's genius is that the 'emperor' is the mirror of earthly governance.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the story where the Jade Emperor creates the zodiac race — the animals' order is the myth. The story's genius is that the 'order' is a story about effort.

name: Amaterasu
teaser: The sun goddess of Shinto — she hid in a cave after a quarrel, plunging the world into darkness, and the other gods lured her out with a mirror and a dance. The Japanese imperial line claims descent from her.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the cave scene and notice what lures her out — her own reflection. The myth's genius is that the 'sun' returns when she sees herself.

name: Susanoo
teaser: The storm god, Amaterasu's wild brother — his rampage caused her to hide, but his slaying of the eight-headed serpent Orochi (with eight barrels of sake) is the most famous dragon fight in Japanese myth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Orochi fight — the god defeats the dragon with alcohol, not a sword. The myth's genius is that the 'storm' god wins by patience.

name: Tsukuyomi
teaser: The moon god who killed the food goddess Uke Mochi in disgust — his punishment was to never see the sun goddess again, which is why day and night are separate.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the creation story and notice the 'separation' — the moon and sun never meet. The myth's genius is that the 'why night is night' is a family quarrel.

name: The Kitsune
teaser: The fox spirit that can shapeshift into beautiful women — the nine-tailed fox is the strongest, and the 'fox wedding' and 'fox fires' are real folk beliefs still told in rural Japan.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a kitsune story and notice the shapeshifting rules — the tail is the tell. The folk tales' genius is that the 'fox' is the boundary between human and animal.

name: The Tengu
teaser: The long-nosed mountain goblins of Japanese folklore — originally bird-like, they became the archetype of the arrogant warrior, and their 'crow-tengu' form inspired the masks in Noh theater.

exploreAction.instruction: Read a tengu story and notice the arrogance — the tengu are punished pride. The folk tales' genius is that the 'demon' is the mirror of the warrior.

name: Yokai
teaser: The umbrella of Japanese folk creatures — hundreds of named spirits, from the umbrella ghost to the neck-stretching Rokurokubi, and the 'yokai' are the origin of most anime monster designs.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the yokai encyclopedia entries and notice the domestic items — the spirits are the household. The folklore's genius is that the 'monsters' are the mundane.

name: The Loch Ness Monster
teaser: The most famous cryptid in the world — the 'Surgeon's Photo' of 1934 was a hoax (a toy submarine), but the legend of a monster in the loch is centuries old, and the lake is deep enough to hide one.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1934 hoax story — the 'photograph' is a toy. The legend's genius is that the 'monster' is the lake's depth.

name: Bigfoot
teaser: The apeman of the Pacific Northwest — the 'Patterson-Gimlin film' of 1967 is the most analyzed hoax or evidence in cryptozoology, and the name 'Sasquatch' comes from a real Salish word.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Patterson-Gimlin story — the 'evidence' is a 59-second film. The legend's genius is that the 'monster' is the forest's silence.

name: The Yeti
teaser: The 'Abominable Snowman' — the name was a mistranslation of a Sherpa phrase, and the 'yeti' footprints are likely melted snow or bear tracks. Edmund Hillary led an expedition hunting one.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1951 footprint expedition — the 'yeti' was a misunderstanding. The legend's genius is that the 'monster' is the mountain.

name: The Chupacabra
teaser: The 'goat sucker' — first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995, the creature became a media phenomenon, and the 'chupacabra' carcasses found since are always mangy dogs or coyotes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1995 Puerto Rico reports — the 'sightings' spread by media. The legend's genius is that the 'monster' is the panic.

name: The Kraken
teaser: The giant squid of Nordic sailors' tales — the 'kraken' was described in a 1755 natural history book as a real animal, and the giant squid was finally filmed alive in 2004.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1755 natural history description — the 'monster' was treated as science. The legend's genius is that the myth became a species.

name: Dragons
teaser: The winged serpent appears in every culture independently — Chinese dragons are wise and bring rain, European dragons hoard gold and breathe fire, and the 'dragon' is the most universal monster.

exploreAction.instruction: Compare a Chinese dragon and a European dragon story — the difference is the theology. The myth's genius is that the 'dragon' is the environment's fear.

name: Unicorns
teaser: The one-horned horse of medieval bestiaries — described by Pliny as a real animal, and the 'unicorn' was the symbol of purity that could only be caught by a virgin.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the medieval bestiary entry — the 'unicorn' was a natural history. The myth's genius is that the 'purity' was the fantasy.

name: Vampires
teaser: The blood-drinking undead of Slavic folklore — the 'vampire' was blamed for epidemics (bodies were exhumed and staked), and Bram Stoker's 1897 novel fixed the modern image.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Slavic exhumation records — the 'vampire' was the plague. The legend's genius is that the 'monster' was the epidemiology.

name: Werewolves
teaser: The human who becomes a wolf at full moon — the curse is medieval, and the real 'werewolf' trials of the 16th century executed people who confessed to lycanthropy under torture.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 16th-century trial records — the 'confessions' were coerced. The legend's genius is that the 'wolf' was the outsider.

name: Zombies
teaser: The 'living dead' of Haitian Vodou — the zombie was a person whose soul was stolen and body enslaved, and the 'zombie' of modern horror is a 20th-century American invention.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Haitian origin and notice the difference — the original zombie is a worker, not a eater. The legend's genius is that the 'monster' was the slavery.

name: Valhalla
teaser: The hall of the slain — Odin's warriors die in battle and feast in Valhalla until Ragnarök, and the 'einherjar' (the honored dead) train daily for a war they know they'll lose.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the description of Valhalla's daily routine — the warriors fight and feast in a loop. The myth's genius is that the 'paradise' is training for the end.

name: The Valkyries
teaser: The 'choosers of the slain' — the warrior women who decide who dies in battle and carry the worthy to Valhalla. Their name means 'choosers of the fallen'.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the oldest skaldic verse about the Valkyries — the 'choice' is the power. The myth's genius is that the 'angels' are the battle's arbiters.

name: The Midgard Serpent
teaser: Jörmungandr — the world serpent that encircles Midgard, biting its own tail. At Ragnarök it fights Thor, and they kill each other, the only balanced duel in the Norse endgame.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Ragnarök duel — Thor and the serpent die together. The myth's genius is that the 'world serpent' is the boundary of the world.

name: Cú Chulainn
teaser: The hound of Ulster — the greatest hero of Irish myth, whose warp-spasm battle frenzy made him a monster on the field, and whose tragic death is one of Celtic myth's greatest stories.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Cattle Raid of Cooley and notice the 'warp-spasm' — the rage is the power and the curse. The legend's genius is that the 'hero' is the rage he can't control.

name: The Children of Lir
teaser: The four children turned into swans for 900 years by a jealous stepmother — the story is a national myth of Ireland, and the swans' final transformation is one of the saddest endings in myth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 900-year exile and notice the time — the children outlive the language. The legend's genius is that the 'curse' is the passage of time itself.

name: Finn MacCool
teaser: The giant warrior whose thumb gave him wisdom when he sucked it — the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland is, per the legend, the remains of his bridge to Scotland.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the causeway legend and notice the 'bridge' — the geology IS the story. The legend's genius is that the landscape is the myth's evidence.

name: The Nibelungenlied
teaser: The German national epic — a dragon-slayer's treasure, a stolen bride, and a massacre. The poem's 'revenge spiral' influenced Wagner's Ring cycle and Tolkien's Silmarillion.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the ending and notice the spiral — every revenge creates the next. The epic's genius is that the 'treasure' is the engine of ruin.

name: The Pied Piper
teaser: The rat-catcher who led away Hamelin's children when the town refused to pay — the story is likely about the Children's Crusade of 1212, when hundreds of children left the town and never returned.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 1284 date on the Hamelin church window — the 'legend' is history. The story's genius is that the 'magic' is the migration.

name: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
teaser: The oldest surviving Japanese narrative — a moon princess found in a bamboo stalk who must return to the moon, and the tale's ending (a letter and an elixir burned on a mountain) explains Mount Fuji's smoke.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
exploreAction.instruction: Read the ending — the emperor's letter and the elixir are the mountain. The tale's genius is that the 'princess' is the moon's longing.

name: The White Snake
teaser: The thousand-year-old snake spirit who marries a human — the tale is one of the four great Chinese folk stories, and the 'White Snake' has been retold in film dozens of times.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the Leifeng Pagoda ending — the 'snake' is imprisoned. The tale's genius is that the 'demon' wife is the most human character.

name: The Butterfly Lovers
teaser: The Chinese Romeo and Juliet — two scholars fall in love, the girl's family forbids the match, and the lovers become butterflies. The story is 1,600 years old.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the ending and notice the transformation — the butterflies are the reunion. The tale's genius is that the 'love' is the metamorphosis.

name: Paul Bunyan
teaser: The lumberjack giant of American tall tales — his blue ox Babe is a legend of the logging camps, and the 'tall tale' genre is America's original myth-making: exaggeration as a way of seeing.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the tallest Paul Bunyan story — the 'facts' are the joke. The tall tale's genius is that the hyperbole IS the landscape.

name: Pecos Bill
teaser: The cowboy who rode a cyclone — raised by coyotes, he lassoed tornadoes, and the 'Pecos Bill' stories are the American west's creation myth in comic form.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the cyclone-riding story — the 'impossible' is the genre. The tall tale's genius is that the west itself was the exaggeration.

name: Zeus
teaser: King of the Olympians who won the sky by lottery after freeing his swallowed siblings — his father Cronus ate every child at birth until Zeus arrived hidden in a swaddle of stones.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Zeus in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Hera
teaser: Queen of the gods whose jealousy shaped more Greek stories than any monster — Zeus once hung her from the sky with anvils tied to her ankles just to end an argument.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Hera in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Poseidon
teaser: God of the sea who lost the sky draw to Zeus and never quite got over it — he sent a flood to settle a land dispute with Athena and built Troy's walls for a wage he was cheated out of.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Poseidon in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Apollo
teaser: God of prophecy who killed the Python at Delphi and took over its oracle — his love affairs ended so badly that even his laurel tree used to be a fleeing woman named Daphne.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Apollo in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Artemis
teaser: Hunter goddess who turned a peeping hunter into a stag to be killed by his own dogs — her temple at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders, twice.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Artemis in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Ares
teaser: The god of war whom even his own father called the most hateful of the Olympians — in one story he was trapped in a bronze jar for thirteen months by giants, and nobody came looking.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Ares in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Aphrodite
teaser: Born from sea foam where Uranus's severed body fell — judges voted her the owner of the golden apple that started the entire Trojan War.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Aphrodite in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Hermes
teaser: Messenger god and patron of thieves who invented the lyre the same day he stole his brother's cattle — while still a newborn.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Hermes in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Hephaestus
teaser: The smith god thrown off Olympus twice — once by each parent — who forged automatons of gold and built traps to catch his wife in bed with Ares, inviting the other gods to watch.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Hephaestus in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Dionysus
teaser: The twice-born god of wine whose mother died asking Zeus for proof of his identity — pirates who kidnapped him once watched their ship sprout vines while their oars turned into snakes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Dionysus in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Demeter
teaser: Harvest goddess whose grief for her missing daughter froze every crop on Earth — she drank an entire barrel of a joke-tender named Baubo to laugh and remember to let spring return.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Demeter in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Persephone
teaser: The queen of the underworld bound by a pomegranate seed rule — eat six seeds in the land of the dead, spend six months there every year. The original seasonal contract.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Persephone in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Pandora
teaser: The first woman, crafted by the gods as beautiful bait — her jar released every evil into the world, and only Hope stayed inside when the lid slammed shut.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Pandora in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Midas
teaser: The king whose golden touch starved him before it enriched him — he washed it away in the Pactolus river, which really did contain gold, and ancient Greeks mined it for centuries.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Midas in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Echo
teaser: The nymph cursed to only repeat others' words — she loved Narcissus but could never speak first, and faded until only her voice remained.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Echo in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Theseus
teaser: The labyrinth-solver who forgot to swap his black sails for white ones — his father, watching the horizon, read the black cloth as death and leapt into the Aegean.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Theseus in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Minotaur
teaser: Half-bull half-man locked in Daedalus's labyrinth and fed Athenian youths yearly — the maze was built so well its architect barely escaped it himself.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Minotaur in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Oedipus
teaser: The man who fled a prophecy straight into it — he solved the Sphinx's riddle, became king, and discovered his queen was his mother, blinding himself when the truth surfaced.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Oedipus in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Achilles
teaser: The near-invincible warrior dipped in immortality by his heel — he refused to fight over an insult, sulked while friends died, then avenged them knowing it meant his own death.

exploreAction.instruction: Read one complete retelling of Achilles in a single sitting, then try explaining its strangest scene to someone else in under a minute — myths this durable survive because they still work on people who know nothing about the culture that told them.

name: Hector
teaser: Troy's greatest defender who faced Achilles knowing he would die — three times they ran the city walls before the gods tricked him into stopping.
